newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rebel Chechen commander still defiant on hostages.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Chechen commander still defiant on hostages.

text.p: Chechen field commander Salman Raduyev, defying the region's separatist leaders, said on Tuesday that nobody could force him to free 21 Russian policemen his men seized on Saturday.

Raduyev, whose dark beard disguises a face disfigured in a shootout earlier this year, also said no hostages would be released on Tuesday, dampening hopes for a quick end to an incident that may damage Chechnya's delicate peace process.

"I have put my troops on red alert," Raduyev told Reuters outside his headquarters in the southern Chechen village of Novye Gordali. "If they (Russian or official Chechen forces) want to fight with me, let them come and we see who wins."

Around 60 of Raduyev's fighters disarmed and seized the policemen, from the central Russian city of Penza, when they tried to stop his motorcade driving into the neighbouring Russian region of Dagestan. Raduyev had planned to attend a meeting of Chechens in Dagestan.

Chechnya's separatist leaders are trying to resolve the hostage crisis swiftly, fearing it could delay the withdrawal of Russian troops from their region as scheduled under a peace accord and disrupt local elections set for January 27.
Russian news agencies reported on Monday that Raduyev, who led a successful raid in Dagestan last January, was ready to free all hostages on Tuesday without any conditions.
But the defiant commander said he would not do this until he won a formal apology from Russia for thwarting his planned trip to Dagestan.
"Maybe I will let some of them free as a gesture of good will but at least 11 will stay here until I get an apology," he said. "Anyway, nothing will happen today," he said on Tuesday.
It was not clear whether the separatist government of Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev could issue orders to Raduyev.

Raduyev claims that Chechnya's former leader Dzhokhar Dudayev, who was reported killed earlier this year in a Russian rocket attack, is still alive and he questions the legality of Yandarbiyev's government.
"I respect them all and listen to them as long as we fight together for Chechnya's independence," Raduyev said. "But if they deviate from this way I will go alone."
A board at the entrance to his headquarters says in a clear challenge to the separatist authorities: "Dzhokhar Dudayev armed forces' general staff".

The secretary of President Boris Yeltsin's policy-making Security Council, Ivan Rybkin, and his deputy Boris Berezovsky discussed the hostage-taking incident by telephone with Chechen officials on Tuesday.
Russia agreed under a peace deal struck on August 31 to withdraw its troops sent to Chechnya in late 1994 to quell the region's independence drive.
Under the deal, the rebels accepted the deferral of a final decision on their region's political status for five years.
The fragility of Chechnya's peace process was also thrown into sharp relief on Tuesday by the murder of six Western medical aid workers.

Five women and one man from the International Committee of the Red Cross were killed in cold blood in their beds in the village of Novye Atagi early on Tuesday. Nobody has claimed responsibility for the attack.
